title: PhD Research Proposal for Europe: Structure and a Worked Example
seoTitle: PhD Research Proposal: Structure and a Worked Example
seoDescription: Structure a PhD research proposal around a real question, evidence, methods and feasibility, with a clearly labelled hypothetical worked example.
intro: A PhD proposal explains a problem, what existing research says and how you would investigate it. Start with the programme's requirements: an advertised project may ask for a different document from a self-proposed doctorate.
description:
A PhD proposal explains a problem, what existing research says and how you would investigate it. Start with the programme's requirements: an advertised project may ask for a different document from a self-proposed doctorate.

First: there is no single European PhD proposal format

A proposal for an independently designed doctoral project is different from an application to a predefined funded PhD vacancy. Requirements vary across countries, universities, doctoral schools and funding schemes. Some vacancies ask for a motivation letter rather than a full proposal. DAAD and Prospects demonstrate why you should follow the particular programme’s instructions.

The core structure, explained

Proposal sectionWhat to write
Working titleName the problem, context and proposed method without promising results.
Background and problemExplain what is established and what remains uncertain, with verifiable citations.
Focused literature reviewCompare a small set of key studies and explain how they shape your question.
Research question and objectivesState one manageable question and measurable sub-objectives.
Methods and evidenceDescribe datasets, participants, materials, models, sampling, evaluation metrics and analysis as relevant.
Feasibility, ethics and risksDiscuss access, consent, safety, data protection and alternatives if your main method fails.
Timeline and milestonesBreak the project into literature, design, research, analysis and writing.
Expected contributionIdentify what would be learned, including how negative results could still be useful.
ReferencesInclude genuine, properly formatted sources, following the department’s style.

Worked example: a hypothetical robotics PhD

Illustrative project title: Evaluating Domain Randomisation for Sim-to-Real Transfer in Mobile Robot Navigation. This is a teaching example, not a claim of an original research gap or a completed study.

Research question

Under which simulated environmental variations, if any, does domain randomisation improve navigation robustness when a policy is transferred from simulation to a physical mobile robot?

Proposed methodology

  1. Review peer-reviewed literature on sim-to-real transfer and navigation evaluation.
  2. Construct a simulation baseline and carefully controlled randomisation conditions.
  3. Evaluate policies on held-out simulated environments using collision rate, success rate and task completion time.
  4. Where equipment and safety approval permit, conduct limited physical-robot trials with predefined stop criteria.
  5. Compare outcomes with uncertainty estimates, investigate failure cases and report null results.

Possible limits

Access to hardware, simulator fidelity, domain shift and safety constraints may restrict generalisability. These limitations belong in the proposal rather than being hidden.

How to use the worked example

The robotics example above is hypothetical and illustrates structure. Adapt the approach to your own question and the programme instructions; do not present its proposed work as results you have achieved.

Tailoring your proposal to the destination

  • Germany: check whether you are applying to an individual doctorate or a structured programme, and whether a professor must agree to supervise.
  • UK: check the project specification, the application portal and whether an advertised studentship has a fixed research topic.
  • Netherlands and Nordic countries: many PhD positions are advertised as employment vacancies; follow the job specification rather than assuming a standalone proposal is needed.
  • EU-funded doctoral networks: check individual recruitment, mobility and eligibility rules at the official vacancy page.

Proposal checklist

  • Does the question fit the advertised area or supervisor’s expertise?
  • Is every empirical claim supported by a real source?
  • Do methods actually answer the question?
  • Have ethics, constraints and contingency plans been addressed?
  • Does the proposal follow the exact word count and required headings?

Check that the methods answer the question

Read each objective beside the experiment or analysis that would address it. If an objective has no method, it is still an intention rather than a plan. If a method does not contribute to an objective, reconsider why it is there. For example, a robotics proposal comparing two controllers needs a shared task, comparable conditions and a defined evaluation. It does not automatically need a large hardware deployment. Explain which observations would support your hypothesis, which would challenge it, and what you would do if the first experiment is inconclusive.

Make every method answer a question

Write the central research question before listing equipment or algorithms. Then ask what observation would help answer it, what data are needed and what comparison would make the result interpretable. A method earns its place because it addresses that question, not because it is fashionable or already familiar to you.

Separate the established background from your interpretation. Cite a paper for what its authors actually investigated and found. If you believe a limitation motivates your study, explain the reasoning and label it as your proposed direction. Do not claim a new research gap merely because a keyword search did not return the same project title.

A feasibility table for the proposed work

Proposed elementFeasibility questionSensible contingency
DatasetCan you obtain permission and suitable coverage?Identify an acceptable alternative before depending on access.
ExperimentAre equipment, time and expertise available?Define a smaller test that still addresses part of the question.
AnalysisWhat assumptions does the method require?State how you will check whether those assumptions hold.
EvaluationWhat baseline and metrics make the result meaningful?Include outcomes that would challenge the hypothesis.

Use the table to strengthen the plan rather than promise that every difficulty is solved. If an essential resource is unconfirmed, say so. A realistic uncertainty is more credible than a confident claim that depends on someone else's equipment or data.

Separate a hypothesis from an expected contribution

A hypothesis is something the study will test. An expected contribution describes what the work could clarify even if the hypothesis is not supported. For a hypothetical robotics study, a proposed controller might fail under a disturbance class; a careful account of that limit can still be informative. Do not write the proposal as though improved performance is already a result.

Build the timeline around work packages with decisions. Reading and setup lead to a baseline; the baseline informs the proposed experiment; evaluation determines the next investigation. Avoid a calendar that simply repeats research, writing and publication without showing how the stages depend on one another.

Does every European PhD need a proposal?

No single European rule applies. Advertised projects, structured programmes and self-proposed doctorates can ask for different materials. Follow the actual call's requirements.

How should I use a worked example?

Use the example to understand how a question, methods and evaluation fit together. Develop your own project from relevant literature and programme instructions; do not present a hypothetical example as research you have completed.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • Sheffield: research proposal structure and methods
